approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would help Commonwealth agencies disrupt the profits of transnational organised criminal groups.
It would change money laundering laws to target the controllers of laundering networks who avoid direct contact with money.
Schedules would also close loopholes for undercover police cautions, stop criminals buying back forfeited property, and clarify that 'benefit' includes avoiding debts or taxes.
Extends money laundering offences to people who cause a criminal dealing with money or property to occur, capturing network controllers.
Creates new offences for dealing with money or property valued at $1,000,000 or more where it is reasonably suspected to be proceeds of indictable crime.
Adds another tier of offences for money or property valued at $10,000,000.
Clarifies that caution and other obligations on investigating officials under Part IC of the Crimes Act do not apply to undercover operatives.
Prevents criminal entities from using buy-back applications for forfeited property and ensures buy-backs are not funded by illicit money or unexplained wealth.
Increases penalties for non-compliance with information-gathering powers under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.
Commonwealth agencies, transnational organised criminal groups, money laundering network controllers, undercover operatives, and the Official Trustee in Bankruptcy.

The Crimes Legislation Amendment (Economic Disruption) Bill 2020 overhauls Commonwealth money-laundering offences, creates new offences targeting controllers and wilful ignorance, adds a tier for laundering $10 million or more, and amends the Proceeds of Crime Act to prevent criminals buying back forfeited property and to clarify definitions, with the direct cost of transnational serious and organised crime estimated at $47.4 billion per year.

The speaker supported the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Economic Disruption) Bill 2020 but moved a second reading amendment criticising the government's slow progress on anti-money-laundering reforms, noting that Australia has not implemented all 2016 recommendations, other jurisdictions are ahead, and AUSTRAC warned in 2017 about regulatory gaps in casino junket operations. The Australian Federal Police restrained over $250 million in criminal assets in the last financial year.

The government argued the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Economic Disruption) Bill 2020 is a key priority to combat organised crime by strengthening money-laundering offences, criminal asset confiscation and controlled operations. The speaker also announced they would table an addendum to the explanatory memorandum in response to comments from the Senate Standing Committee for the Scrutiny of Bills.
